title: What makes a territory-control mechanic fun when players can lose what they've claimed?
author: Limp_Light_4144
selftext:
I've been working on a game called Wibto, where players claim hexes on a real-world map by walking or running. Other players can capture those hexes, which creates a cycle of expanding territory and trying to reclaim lost areas.

I recently switched the game to a hex-based territory system, and it's got me thinking about the design problem behind it.

If players can lose territory they've worked to claim, that creates competition and a reason to return. But if losing territory feels too punishing, players might just give up instead.

Where's the balance between making territory worth fighting for and making players feel like their progress is constantly being taken away?

I'm especially interested in how other games handle territory loss, comeback mechanics, and defending what you've built.

**Google Play:** [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.wibto](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.wibto)

**App Store:** [https://apps.apple.com/us/app/wibto/id6753147272](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/wibto/id6753147272)

comments.author: joeld42
comments.body: Hey this is a classic question in area control games. It's about rearranging the decision to be "how much effort/resources/whatever is it worth it to me to control this area". If you haven't played many tabletop area control games, you might want to try some of those, "Small World" might be a good one to start with as it's all about losing and regaining the same territory (plus it's pretty fun). There's a digital version of it on Steam too. I think one of the ways you could address it is having each run reinforce instead of just claim the territory, and making it more about claiming it "when a specific event occurs" (such as a reset). For example, you could build "city states" out of the groups of neighboring hexes and have each citystate award  points to the to 3 people in at at the end of a reset, but have them all reset at different times, you might have high-frequency areas with heavy traffic that reset every day or two, and larger, low-traffic areas that reset every few weeks or months.  Also, look for ways to make it not "zero-sum" as that feels punishing, if you're designing the system there's no reason why two players can't both claim a piece of territory. It's not a gold mine that only one person can hoard, the gold mine can give every one who visits that week some gold. Having some competition does create incentive and strategy but you get to decide where that line is.

replies.author: Limp_Light_4144
replies.body: Thanks, these are some really interesting ideas. I like the city-state concept and the idea of making territory less zero-sum. I will definitely check out Small World too
